analysis.one_liner: Gives disabled people a federally protected right to get long-term care at home instead of in institutions.
analysis.headline: The bill had 238 cosponsors, including 221 of 231 House Democrats and 17 of 197 House Republicans, but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it discrimination for governments and long-term care insurers to force people with disabilities into nursing homes or other institutions when they could live at home with help. It would require community-based services to be offered before anyone is institutionalized, require states to plan and report on moving people out of institutions, and push for enough affordable, accessible housing so people actually have somewhere to live. States that comply would get a bonus in federal Medicaid matching funds, and individuals could sue to enforce their rights.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need help with daily living and qualify for institutional care — they could get services in their own homes and communities instead. Family caregivers and home care workers also benefit, since the bill requires payment rates sufficient to sustain a home care workforce, and it funds home modifications and caregiver supports.

how_it_helps.text: Bars government entities and long-term care insurers from denying, capping, or putting waiting lists on community-based services for people who would otherwise qualify for institutional placement [S2, S3].
Requires community-based services to be offered before institutionalization and requires that institutionalized people be regularly told about community alternatives [S2, S3].

Requires states to plan for shifting funding from institutions to community services with measurable annual targets, and to ensure availability of affordable, accessible, integrated housing — including funding home modifications [S2, S3].
Gives compliant states a 5 percentage point increase in the federal Medicaid match for home and community-based services, so the federal government shares the cost of the shift [S3].
Lets individuals sue for damages and injunctions, appoints attorneys for people who cannot afford one, and directs the Attorney General to investigate and enforce violations [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments and long-term care insurers would bear new obligations: states would have to shift funding away from institutional care, build up community service capacity, and secure affordable accessible housing, while private long-term care insurers would face new service mandates, self-evaluations, and lawsuits. The nursing home industry would lose business as funding shifts to home and community care.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes large new obligations on states without a broad new funding stream; the only financial sweetener is a 5-point Medicaid match increase tied to meeting the transition plan, so states would have to find much of the money themselves, mostly by shifting it out of institutional care [S3].

The housing requirement may outrun reality: states must guarantee sufficient affordable, accessible, integrated housing, but the bill does not appropriate money to build it, and accessible affordable housing is already scarce [S2, S3].

Private lawsuits with damages, appointed attorneys, and no filing fees could push providers and insurers into costly litigation while standards are still being set by regulations due 24 months after enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, the bill offers something no other law provides: an enforceable right to live at home rather than be placed in an institution. The genuine cost falls on states, which would have to reorganize long-term care funding over up to 12 years, and on the institutional care industry. The design mitigates this with the federal match bonus and a long transition timeline, but the unfunded housing mandate is the weakest part.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees and then to their subcommittees on Health and on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, and it sat there — no markup, no vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 15, 2019 by Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI) [S3].
It attracted 238 cosponsors — 221 of 231 House Democrats and 17 of 197 House Republicans — giving it more named backers than a majority of the House [S4].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees on January 15, 2019, then to the Health Subcommittee on January 25 and the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties Subcommittee on February 25 [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no subcommittee vote, no committee markup, no floor vote, before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home and institutional care providers keep their funding stream, and state Medicaid budgets avoided a mandate to shift billions toward home and community care. People with disabilities who need long-term care gained nothing; they remain without a federal statutory right to live in their communities.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing homes and state Medicaid budgets

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan and near-universal among Democrats — 221 of 231 signed on, along with 17 of 197 Republicans — and no opponent is recorded anywhere in the bill's history; the bill died of inaction, not a vote.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill requires public entities to set annual targets for shifting funding from institutional settings to home and community-based services and to move people out of institutions [S3]. That redirects Medicaid dollars away from the institutional care industry and toward care people choose themselves.

industries.industry: Home and community-based care agencies and home care workers
industries.note: States must ensure payment rates sufficient to sustain a workforce that supports people living at home, and must fund home modifications and caregiver supports [S3]. Demand for home care would grow substantially.

The bill directly regulates long-term care insurers, requiring them to offer and provide community-based services, run public participation processes, keep self-evaluations on file, and face suits with damages [S3]. Some of what they would be required to fund (home care) costs less than the institutional care they currently pay for, but the mandates and litigation exposure are real.

States must submit transition plans, guarantee affordable accessible housing, and fund community services, but compliant states earn a 5 percentage point increase in the federal Medicaid match for home and community-based services, and the transition runs up to 12 years [S2, S3].
